Therefore a brief consideration of its fruit is now begun.
mv-k05-v688.inference: Having established perception's supremacy, the discussion turns to its practical result.

mv-k05-v689.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v689.question: Is talk of difference compatible with the true fruit of cognition?
premises: Cognition itself is essentially reflective awareness.
The fruit of cognition must accord with that essential nature.
Talk of difference does not fit that fruit.
mv-k05-v689.inference: Because cognition is reflective awareness, difference-based accounts are not suited to its fruit.

mv-k05-v690.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v690.question: What is the ultimate fruit if practical cognitions like avoidance are considered?
premises: One might propose avoidance and similar cognitions as the fruit.
Even those arise from manifestation.
Alternatively, ultimate awareness is self-luminous.
mv-k05-v690.inference: Even practical fruits depend on manifestation, pointing back to self-luminous awareness as ultimate.

mv-k05-v691.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v691.question: What is the final and primary fruit recognized everywhere in this system?
premises: That self-luminous awareness is the final fruit everywhere.
This is well determined.
Joy and similar experiences, spoken of as primary fruits, are included within it.
mv-k05-v691.inference: The ultimate fruit is self-luminous awareness, within which joy and other fruits are subsumed.

mv-k05-v692.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v692.question: Where does the primary fruit of joy ultimately come to rest?
premises: Joy and similar fruits come to rest in one's own awareness.
That awareness is the full self.
Thus perception expands on all sides as this awareness.
mv-k05-v692.inference: All experiential fruits culminate in repose within the full self-awareness, which is perception itself.

mv-k05-v693.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v693.question: What accomplishments arise for one devoted to the practice of this perception?
premises: One may be devoted to the practice of this perception.
Such devotion leads to accomplishments.
These include hearing from afar, inclined toward what is spoken by Brahma and others, beginning from kala and so on.
mv-k05-v693.inference: Practice of this perception yields extraordinary accomplishments, including distant hearing.
uncertainties: The compound brahmādibhāṣitaśrautapraunmukhyena is dense; the sense is an inclination toward hearing what is spoken by Brahma and others.

mv-k05-v694.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v694.question: What specific powers arise from devotion to this perceptual practice?
premises: Hearing-cognition from afar arises quickly.
Even in an aspect of a thing seen only by the mind, clear cognition arises.
These arise abundantly through the practice.
mv-k05-v694.inference: The practice produces both distant sensory cognition and clear mental cognition.

mv-k05-v695.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v695.question: Why is the arising of clear cognition unsurprising when overcome by the power of self-reflection?
premises: When something is overcome by the power of one's own reflective awareness, extraordinary cognition can arise.
Such arising is not surprising.
The Spanda scripture states this for an attentive mind.
mv-k05-v695.inference: The power of self-reflection naturally produces heightened cognition, as confirmed by the Spanda tradition.

mv-k05-v696.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v696.question: How does the discussion conclude regarding perception and the universe of the supreme lord?
premises: The Spanda scripture says that in an attentive mind it shines forth ever more clearly.
Further elaboration is unnecessary.
In this way, this entire universe is indeed perception belonging to the supreme lord.
mv-k05-v696.inference: The universe is nothing other than the supreme lord's perception, shining with increasing clarity.

mv-k05-v697.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v697.question: Why does no confusion of cognitions arise despite an undivided group of knowers?
premises: The group of knowers remains undivided even in diverse cognitions.
Cognitions are connected with distinct modes of manifestation.
Distinct manifestation prevents the mixing of cognitions.
mv-k05-v697.inference: Therefore no confusion of cognitions occurs even though the knowers are undivided.

mv-k05-v698.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v698.question: How can perception remain distinct when its field is the same?
premises: Perception may operate in an equal or shared field.
The cognitions of pot and non-pot do not become the same.
Perception manifests with its own unmistakable clarity.
mv-k05-v698.inference: Therefore perception expands without rival even when its field is shared.

mv-k05-v699.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v699.question: What follows from perception's undivided manifestation of objects?
premises: The object is not divided in the act of perception.
Perception reveals a nondual unity of awareness and object.
This is understood by a mind established in unifying insight.
mv-k05-v699.inference: Therefore such nonduality of perception is affirmed.

mv-k05-v700.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v700.question: What contrasting views are presented about perception and inference?
premises: Teacher Narasiṃha teaches the nonduality of perception.
Some others claim inference is the valid means for the whole universe.
These positions represent different accounts of valid knowledge.
mv-k05-v700.inference: The verse sets up a contrast between perceptual nonduality and inference-based epistemology.

mv-k05-v701.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v701.question: Why does the all-knowing Lord not enter ordinary practical usage?
premises: The Lord is all-knowing and of nonconceptual nature.
Even as perceptual in nature, he does not become an object of ordinary usage.
Practical usage requires conceptual determination.
mv-k05-v701.inference: Therefore the Lord's nonconceptual awareness does not directly function in ordinary practical dealings.

mv-k05-v702.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v702.question: How can conceptual practical activity arise within the nonconceptual?
premises: Practical activity is conceptual in nature.
The nonconceptual does not itself operate through concepts.
All ordinary practical activity is carried on through conceptualization.
mv-k05-v702.inference: Therefore practical activity cannot arise directly from the nonconceptual without conceptual mediation.

mv-k05-v703.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v703.question: What conceptual structures belong to inference as a means of knowledge?
premises: Inference operates through conceptual constructions.
Its constructions include subject, property, pervasion, and their apprehension.
These elements together constitute inferential cognition.
mv-k05-v703.inference: Therefore inference is identified with a set of conceptual constructions.

mv-k05-v704.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v704.question: How can inference operate if perception is ultimately absent?
premises: In ultimate reality there is only one cognition.
Inference is commonly thought to depend on prior perception.
An objection arises about inference in the absence of perception.
mv-k05-v704.inference: The verse raises the problem of how inference is possible if only one ultimate cognition exists.

mv-k05-v705.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v705.question: What ultimately grounds the connection required for inference?
premises: Inference is said to depend on a connection determined by perception.
That dependence is conceded at the empirical level.
Ultimately there is one Lord who is the abode of omniscience.
mv-k05-v705.inference: The grounding of inferential connection is traced back to the one omniscient Lord.

mv-k05-v706.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v706.question: How does pervasion become established in awareness?
premises: Pervasion becomes possible in awareness through immersion in the Lord.
Without that grounding, relations like fire and smoke cannot be reliably known.
Knowledge of presence and absence depends on a deeper awareness.
mv-k05-v706.inference: Therefore inferential pervasion is grounded in participation in the Lord's awareness.

mv-k05-v707.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v707.question: Why would agreement and difference fail without a deeper grounding?
premises: Agreement and difference cannot be established by mere repetition over long time.
Inferential recognition depends on similarity grasped by a primary cognition.
That primary cognition provides the basis for comparison.
mv-k05-v707.inference: Therefore agreement and difference depend on a primary cognition grounded in similarity.

mv-k05-v708.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v708.question: What do all knowing subjects ultimately depend on for inference and action?
premises: Inference is declared to be what sets practical activity in motion.
All knowing subjects operate within practical activity.
Their operation depends on the Lord's awareness present everywhere.
mv-k05-v708.inference: Therefore all knowers depend on the Lord's universal awareness for inference and practical life.

mv-k05-v709.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v709.question: How could ignorant beings become knowers without entering that awareness?
premises: Beings come to the state of being knowers by depending on the Lord's awareness.
Without that dependence, their knowerhood is not explained.
The class of beings is otherwise ignorant.
mv-k05-v709.inference: Therefore ignorant beings cannot attain knowerhood without participation in that awareness.

mv-k05-v710.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v710.question: Is connection with awareness difficult for a being to attain?
premises: A being attains the nature of a knower only through awareness.
Without that awareness, knowerhood cannot arise.
Connection with awareness is therefore essential and not difficult in principle.
mv-k05-v710.inference: Therefore a being's connection with awareness is necessary and not hard to obtain.

mv-k05-v711.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v711.question: What is the true status of a knower in relation to the Lord's perception?
premises: In reality no knower exists apart from awareness.
Every knower has awareness as its lord.
Any valid position derives its operation from the Lord's perception.
mv-k05-v711.inference: Therefore the knower's position is grounded in the Lord's perceptual awareness.

mv-k05-v712.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v712.question: Why is bound knowledge described as dependent and limited?
premises: Bound knowledge depends on something other than itself.
The bound being is ignorant and not sovereign.
Such a being does not control its own pleasure and pain.
mv-k05-v712.inference: Therefore the bound means of knowing is dependent and limited.

mv-k05-v713.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v713.question: What epistemic position did the sage declare about bound beings?
premises: The bound being acts as impelled by the Lord.
A sage declared this dependence explicitly.
From that view, inference dependent on the Lord becomes the sole means of knowing.
mv-k05-v713.inference: Therefore the sage upheld inference dependent on the Lord as the sole valid means for bound beings.

mv-k05-v714.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v714.question: How did later thinkers respond to the inference-based position?
premises: The teacher named Lolaṭa determined a widely accepted position.
Another thinker took up that position.
That thinker conceded some validity to perceptual awareness.
mv-k05-v714.inference: The inference-based view was influential but prompted partial concession to perception.

mv-k05-v715.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v715.question: Can inference be fully certain when error is so easy in it?
premises: Perceptual awareness has validity in practical activity.
Inference is prone to easy deviation or error.
Certainty is difficult where deviation is common.
mv-k05-v715.inference: Therefore inference is questioned as a fully certain means of valid knowledge.

mv-k05-v716.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v716.question: Who could confidently rely on agreement and difference as decisive proof?
premises: A careful examiner seeks certainty before resting in a conclusion.
Agreement and difference depend on presence in similar and dissimilar cases.
Such dependence raises doubts about their decisiveness.
mv-k05-v716.inference: Therefore a critical examiner cannot confidently rest on agreement and difference alone.

mv-k05-v717.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v717.question: Why do initial observations fail to produce certainty in inference?
premises: What is seen at first does not by itself establish certainty.
Inference is vulnerable to faults such as defects in the subject-property relation.
Such faults justify rejecting premature certainty.
mv-k05-v717.inference: Therefore initial agreement and difference do not yield certainty because of inferential defects.
uncertainties: The final token 'ṇam' appears fragmentary in the transmitted text.

mv-k05-v718.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v718.question: What is the practical status of inference if it cannot yield certainty?
premises: Trying to secure certainty from faulty inference is compared to purifying filth with dust.
Inference often leaves room for doubt.
Doubt can still prompt practical action.
mv-k05-v718.inference: Therefore inference remains as doubt that may still serve as an aid to action.

mv-k05-v719.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v719.question: Why is the bound being's means of knowing associated with māyā?
premises: Doubtful cognition manifests difference.
What manifests difference is designated as māyā.
Bound beings know through a means born of māyā and consciousness.
mv-k05-v719.inference: Therefore the bound being's means of knowing is māyā-based because it manifests difference.
uncertainties: The compound 'māyācidātakam' is interpreted as 'born of māyā and consciousness' based on context.

mv-k05-v720.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v720.question: What role does reasoning play when certainty is unavailable?
premises: Reasoning considers the possibility that one side of an issue may stand.
It weighs the greater force of benefit or harm.
Such weighing can guide engagement or withdrawal in action.
mv-k05-v720.inference: Therefore reasoning functions pragmatically to guide action when certainty is lacking.
uncertainties: The token 'ttyai' appears fragmentary in the transmitted text and is read in relation to 'pravṛttau'.

mv-k05-v721.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v721.question: Why is Śiva alone the true knower without other means of knowledge?
premises: Śiva is all-powerful and the sole knower.
This entire knowable world is his own limb.
Other ostentatious means of knowledge are unnecessary.
mv-k05-v721.inference: Because the whole field of knowledge is Śiva's own manifestation, he alone is the self-sufficient knower.

mv-k05-v722.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v722.question: How does the bound soul's knowledge differ from Śiva's manifestation?
premises: For Śiva, the knowable appears as fully determinate certainty.
Every other being is a bound soul.
The bound soul remains in the darkness of doubt.
mv-k05-v722.inference: Unlike Śiva's certain manifestation, the bound soul's cognition is enveloped in doubt.

mv-k05-v723.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v723.question: What kind of certainty does the bound soul attain in doubt?
premises: The bound soul is colored by a flash-like awareness.
This awareness considers two opposing alternatives.
It reaches a determination of one side as true or the other as otherwise.
mv-k05-v723.inference: The bound soul's certainty is a fleeting, alternative-based determination rather than stable knowledge.

mv-k05-v724.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v724.question: Why does reasoning fail to provide stable certainty for practical activity?
premises: Even when finding a conclusion, one does not gain firm grounding in it.
All practical activity proceeds from such reasoning.
This is the established condition of ordinary conduct.
mv-k05-v724.inference: Because reasoning yields no firm grounding, all ordinary practical activity rests on unstable deliberation.

mv-k05-v725.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v725.question: What makes this form of knowledge impure as a means of knowledge?
premises: This knowledge should be designated as an impure means of knowledge.
Its impurity has a specific extent.
That impurity consists in not conforming to the real object.
mv-k05-v725.inference: The knowledge is impure because it does not faithfully follow the nature of reality.

mv-k05-v726.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v726.question: What do other thinkers propose as the driving factor behind activity?
premises: Others hold that one without a purpose does not act.
They identify needfulness as the sole assistant to action.
On this basis they argue for a different account of cognition.
mv-k05-v726.inference: For these thinkers, purposive need, not mere reasoning, explains why activity occurs.

mv-k05-v727.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v727.question: How do different schools explain the role of desire and doubt in prompting action?
premises: Some who know the self as other assign the status of a means of knowledge to desire.
Others claim that even doubt does not arise about something wholly undetermined.
The example of an elephant illustrates the need for some prior determination.
mv-k05-v727.inference: These views suggest that action requires either desire or some minimal determination, not sheer indeterminacy.

mv-k05-v728.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v728.question: What minimal awareness enables people to act according to this view?
premises: Desire or activity arises only when some capability is present.
People notice their own agency, even slightly.
This slight awareness supports their continual engagement in action.
mv-k05-v728.inference: A minimal recognition of one's own agency is sufficient to initiate ordinary activity.

mv-k05-v729.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v729.question: How does the power of limited agency explain action regardless of the object's status?
premises: People engage in action through the unfolding of kalā, the power of limited agency.
Through kalā they assume agency in themselves.
The external object may or may not actually be as conceived.
mv-k05-v729.inference: Action is grounded in the subject's limited agency rather than in the object's independent reality.

mv-k05-v730.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v730.question: What alternative explanation do others give for the source of practical activity?
premises: One who assumes agency acts everywhere.
Others point to a beginningless practical tradition.
That tradition is inherently constituted by action.
mv-k05-v730.inference: Some explain activity not by individual cognition but by an beginningless stream of conventional practice.

mv-k05-v731.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v731.question: How is the beginningless tradition identified with cosmic restriction and scripture?
premises: Niyati abides as the impelling principle of the whole world.
That same principle is called scripture.
Scripture is identified with the traditional practice of the elders.
mv-k05-v731.inference: The regulating power of the world, scripture, and ancestral convention are presented as one continuous authority.

mv-k05-v732.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v732.question: Why is the determination of dharma said to come from tradition rather than perception or inference?
premises: The complete determination of dharma and related matters is at issue.
Perception and inference do not reliably establish it.
Such means are often deceptive in these matters.
mv-k05-v732.inference: Therefore the settled understanding of dharma is grounded in authoritative tradition rather than ordinary epistemic means.

mv-k05-v733.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v733.question: How do even examining minds come to trust received knowledge?
premises: Even those inclined to examination develop trust.
Children learn from others that food removes hunger and water removes thirst.
Such trust arises from received testimony and experience.
mv-k05-v733.inference: Confidence in knowledge often begins from authoritative transmission before independent verification.

mv-k05-v734.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v734.question: How does trust in testimony extend to other domains of knowledge?
premises: People ascertain some things from another source.
They do not doubt those things once accepted.
They then rely on that same source in other matters, including perception-based ones.
mv-k05-v734.inference: Authoritative transmission can function as a primary basis that shapes confidence even in other domains.

mv-k05-v735.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v735.question: What role does scripture play for examiners in determining merit and demerit?
premises: Even examiners obtain proper certainty from what scripture declares.
The sage speaks of merit and demerit as a pair.
These matters require authoritative instruction.
mv-k05-v735.inference: Scriptural teaching provides the decisive basis for determining merit and demerit.

mv-k05-v736.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v736.question: What is the true nature of scripture beyond written texts?
premises: The purpose of ordinary teaching texts is limited.
Scripture is not merely a collection of books.
Scripture has a deeper authoritative function.
mv-k05-v736.inference: Scripture must be understood as more than its written textual form.

mv-k05-v737.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v737.question: How is scripture identified with beginningless linguistic tradition?
premises: Scripture is not merely the famous Veda and similar texts.
It is fundamentally an established tradition.
That tradition has the nature of speech.
mv-k05-v737.inference: Scripture is best understood as a beginningless, speech-formed tradition rather than a bounded textual corpus.

mv-k05-v738.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v738.question: How pervasive is the linguistic tradition across different religious systems?
premises: The speech-based tradition appears in all philosophical and religious views.
It never comes to be rejected.
It includes the shared vocabulary of diverse practices and symbols.
mv-k05-v738.inference: The authority of tradition is shown by its universal and unrejected presence across all systems.

mv-k05-v739.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v739.question: What range of practices is encompassed by the shared traditional vocabulary?
premises: The tradition names ascetic, ritual, and domestic practices.
Its vocabulary spans severe austerities and household life.
These terms function across different religious contexts.
mv-k05-v739.inference: The breadth of this vocabulary demonstrates the comprehensive reach of the speech-based tradition.

mv-k05-v740.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v740.question: How can the meanings of such traditional terms be understood without established usage?
premises: Many religious and practical terms derive meaning from tradition.
Understanding requires grasping both one's own and others' uses.
No alternative means is available apart from established usage.
mv-k05-v740.inference: Established linguistic tradition is indispensable for understanding the meanings of such terms.

mv-k05-v741.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v741.question: Why do the wise regard scripture as a valid means of knowledge?
premises: Scripture is identified with established tradition.
That tradition is a form of divine speech.
It is authoritative because it does not deviate.
mv-k05-v741.inference: The wise accept scripture as a valid means of knowledge because it is non-deviating divine tradition.

mv-k05-v742.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v742.question: Does scripture remain authoritative whether or not it appears reasonable?
premises: Scripture is well known in the world.
It may appear reasonable or otherwise.
It functions in domains of both knowledge and ignorance.
mv-k05-v742.inference: Scripture's authority is established independently of whether it seems reasonable in a given case.

mv-k05-v743.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v743.question: What principle do others propose instead of restriction to explain authoritative order?
premises: Some assign authoritativeness to niyati for certain inhabitants.
Others propose a distinct principle.
They identify that principle as time.
mv-k05-v743.inference: The debate shifts from restriction to time as the ordering principle behind experience and authority.
uncertainties: The referent of śrīmadbhūtajāntanivāsinām is context-specific and not fully clear from this verse alone.

mv-k05-v744.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v744.question: How does time differentiate present clarity from past non-clarity?
premises: The present operates with a clearly manifest nature.
The past is characterized by a formerly clear aspect that is now not manifest.
Time accounts for this difference in manifestation.
mv-k05-v744.inference: Time is presented as the principle that structures the shift between manifest clarity and non-manifestation.

mv-k05-v745.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v745.question: Why can past and future time not be established as independent realities?
premises: The past is conceived by assuming a cause.
The future is conceived as something yet to come.
Neither past nor future can stand on its own because each depends on the other.
mv-k05-v745.inference: Past and future lack independent existence due to mutual dependence.

mv-k05-v746.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v746.question: What further faults undermine the independent reality of time?
premises: Positing time leads to infinite regress.
Observed forms reverse and change, preventing a stable temporal form.
Time lacks a fixed measure and depends on both subject and object.
mv-k05-v746.inference: These defects show that time cannot be established as an independent reality.

mv-k05-v747.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v747.question: Why does time fail to have a coherent intrinsic nature?
premises: Time never appears in an unconditioned form.
Time cannot be consistently defined as one or many.
Time cannot be consistently defined as permanent or impermanent.
mv-k05-v747.inference: Time lacks a coherent intrinsic nature.

mv-k05-v748.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v748.question: Why is time unnecessary for explaining action and its limiting conditions?
premises: If one thing has one limiting condition, unity alone does not require time.
If difference arises within action or its condition, that difference is explained internally.
Time adds no explanatory function in either case.
mv-k05-v748.inference: Time is explanatorily redundant with respect to action and its conditions.
uncertainties: The token '(?)' marks a textual uncertainty in the transmitted reading.

mv-k05-v749.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v749.question: Why does attributing difference to time fail whether time or another cause produces it?
premises: If time produces difference, the account falls into infinite regress.
If another cause produces difference through mutual dependence, the same regress follows.
Conditioned difference is not ultimately real or substantial.
mv-k05-v749.inference: Difference cannot establish time as a real independent principle.

mv-k05-v750.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k05-v750.question: How does consciousness account for presentness without positing time as an independent principle?
premises: Time cannot be established as a produced effect.
A single undivided entity does not require time for its function.
Consciousness itself gives vividness, presentness, and enduring presence.
mv-k05-v750.inference: The appearance of the present is grounded in consciousness rather than in an independent time.
uncertainties: The compound 'sphuṭatādattavartamānasadātvataḥ' is compact; the gloss follows the most plausible reading in this argumentative context.

mv-k06-v751.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v751.question: How does the lord of consciousness manifest time?
premises: Past and future dissolve into the present moment.
The present itself also dissolves in consciousness.
The lord of consciousness is the agent who manifests time.
mv-k06-v751.inference: Because past, future, and present all dissolve in consciousness, time is fully manifested by the lord of consciousness alone.

mv-k06-v752.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v752.question: What is the nature of transmigration for consciousness that manifests time?
premises: The lord of consciousness manifests time as its own appearance.
Transmigration arises within that same consciousness.
Transmigration contains the manifestation of consciousness's own nature.
mv-k06-v752.inference: For consciousness whose nature manifests time, transmigration is the play of being and nonbeing appearing within its own form.

mv-k06-v753.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v753.question: How is the unfolding of knowerhood described in its own form?
premises: Abiding in its own form is the unfolding of knowerhood.
Knowerhood involves the distinction between 'I' and 'this'.
It also involves negations such as 'not this' and further determinations like 'that'.
mv-k06-v753.inference: The unfolding of knowerhood is the dynamic abiding in one's own form through affirmations and negations of 'I', 'this', and 'that'.

mv-k06-v754.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v754.question: What is the status of pure knowerhood in relation to the manifestation of nonbeing?
premises: The cognition 'this is not this' is a varied manifestation of nonbeing.
Supreme knowerhood is pure in itself.
In pure knowerhood there is no separate abiding of such distinctions.
mv-k06-v754.inference: The varied play of nonbeing belongs to manifestation, but pure knowerhood itself does not contain separate abiding of those distinctions.

mv-k06-v755.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v755.question: Why is isolated pure knowerhood insufficient to explain worldly cognition?
premises: In the purely isolated aspect of knowerhood there is no cognition as such.
Worldly knowerhood always involves determinate cognition.
Worldly knowerhood is therefore of a different, differentiated kind.
mv-k06-v755.inference: Pure isolated knowerhood cannot account for cognition, whereas all worldly knowerhood is constituted by such differentiated cognition.

mv-k06-v756.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v756.question: What makes the cognition of nonbeing possible?
premises: Nonbeing can appear as an object of cognition.
Such appearance depends on the operation of time.
The absolute consciousness is perfectly full and contains all forms.
mv-k06-v756.inference: The cognition of nonbeing is possible because the perfectly full consciousness, through time, manifests even absence within itself.

mv-k06-v757.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v757.question: Can knower, knowing, and known stand as independently real entities?
premises: Knower, cognition, and known are mutually defined roles.
If they were absolutely real, their status would not be relative.
Their actual functioning depends on mutual relation.
mv-k06-v757.inference: Knower, cognition, and known cannot stand as independently real entities because their status is inherently relative.

mv-k06-v758.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v758.question: Why can the knower not be established independently of the known?
premises: The being of the knower is conceived only in relation to the known.
If their mutual form is absent, the relation cannot be established.
If their mutual form is present, independence is still impossible because of incompatibility.
mv-k06-v758.inference: The knower cannot be established independently, since its being depends on the known in every case.

mv-k06-v759.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v759.question: What further problems arise if knower and known are taken as independently real?
premises: Independent reality would lead to overextension everywhere.
It would wrongly entail omniscience and similar properties.
Noncontributing factors do not manifest simultaneously as required.
mv-k06-v759.inference: Treating knower and known as independently real creates logical overreach and impossible consequences.

mv-k06-v760.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v760.question: Why does deriving knowerhood from another object fail to explain it?
premises: Knowerhood might be thought to arise from another known object.
That explanation would require yet another source for that state.
The resulting state would remain equivalent to something unarisen.
mv-k06-v760.inference: Explaining knowerhood through another known object leads to regress and leaves knowerhood effectively unestablished.

mv-k06-v761.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v761.question: How does the full consciousness give rise to the division of I and this?
premises: The ultimate reality is full consciousness, Shiva.
That consciousness can differentiate its own aspects.
The division into 'not I' and 'this' arises within that differentiation.
mv-k06-v761.inference: The division between subject and object is a constructed differentiation within the one full consciousness.

mv-k06-v762.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v762.question: How do the senses of I and not-I arise within the self?
premises: The self contains the fullness of all that is other than any limited part.
The sense 'I' arises by appropriating that fullness to itself.
The sense 'not I' arises by withdrawing fullness from what is taken as other.
mv-k06-v762.inference: The experiences of 'I' and 'not I' are complementary movements of appropriation and withdrawal within the one self.

mv-k06-v763.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v763.question: How do the I-part and this-part relate to each other in cognition?
premises: The I-part and the this-part arise together in cognition.
Each part excludes the other in its own functioning.
The I-part can conceal the this-part within its own domain.
mv-k06-v763.inference: The I and this aspects of experience are mutually exclusive yet dynamically related within the same cognition.

mv-k06-v764.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v764.question: Does concealment in cognition destroy the concealed object?
premises: The I-aspect can conceal the this-aspect in cognition.
Concealment does not dissolve or annihilate what is concealed.
The concealed object remains established in cognition, though bound by convention.
mv-k06-v764.inference: Cognitive concealment is like covering, not destruction; the concealed remains present within cognition.

mv-k06-v765.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v765.question: How do the I and this arise through mutual exclusion?
premises: The sense of 'this' arises through inner contraction that excludes the I-part.
The sense of 'I' arises through exclusion of the mass of thisness.
Both arise from within the same consciousness.
mv-k06-v765.inference: The poles of 'I' and 'this' are formed by reciprocal exclusion within one inner field of consciousness.

mv-k06-v766.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v766.question: What underlies the manifestation of successive exclusions of I and other?
premises: Experience involves exclusion of one's own I and of other I-senses.
These exclusions manifest in patterned forms.
They proceed by depending on six deities characterized as empty forms.
mv-k06-v766.inference: The play of mutual exclusions operates through six empty-form deities that structure manifestation.
uncertainties: The precise identity of the six deities is not specified in this verse.

mv-k06-v767.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v767.question: How are conceptual construction and time related in manifestation?
premises: The cognition 'that is indeed this' is called conceptual construction.
Time is that by which the universe is articulated.
The universe is articulated through the arising of its own limited parts.
mv-k06-v767.inference: Conceptual construction and time are the same differentiating power by which the universe appears as articulated parts.

mv-k06-v768.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v768.question: What is the luminous aspect present within differentiated manifestation?
premises: Within the differentiated part there is an aspect of manifestation.
That aspect is self-luminous.
As the form of being, it animates all appearances.
mv-k06-v768.inference: Even within differentiation there remains a self-luminous aspect whose nature is to animate all manifestation.

mv-k06-v769.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v769.question: How is the aspect of nonbeing characterized in relation to knower, knowing, and known?
premises: The luminous aspect is not defined as knower, cognition, or known.
There is also an aspect connected with emptiness.
That aspect appears as nonbeing and is associated with Rudra.
mv-k06-v769.inference: Beyond the triad of knower, knowing, and known, manifestation includes an emptiness-aspect of nonbeing associated with Rudra.

mv-k06-v770.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v770.question: How does nonbeing become cognition and give rise to the triad?
premises: The emptiness-aspect associated with Rudra can become cognition.
Through its connection, knowerhood is oriented and articulated.
From cognition the known becomes distinguished as separate.
mv-k06-v770.inference: The same underlying aspect becomes cognition and thereby unfolds into knower, knowing, and known.
uncertainties: The compound mātṛtābhāvivataḥ is morphologically compressed; analysis follows the transmitted fused form.

mv-k06-v771.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v771.question: Who understood time in this way as a mode of cognition?
premises: The preceding verses established time as a mode of cognition.
This understanding was received within a specific teaching lineage.
The lineage is identified by devotion to the guru called Bhavatī.
mv-k06-v771.inference: The doctrine that time is a mode of cognition was understood by those who served the revered guru known as Bhavatī.
uncertainties: The exact identity of the guru called Bhavatī is not specified in this verse.

mv-k06-v772.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v772.question: What is the group of six sheaths said to do in the individual self?
premises: The individual self shines with the joy of consciousness's nature.
A group of six factors is declared in that context.
These six are called the sheaths and are associated with giving knowerhood.
mv-k06-v772.inference: The six sheaths are the limiting factors that confer finite knowerhood upon the individual self.

mv-k06-v773.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v773.question: How do different thinkers explain the cognitive role of the six sheaths?
premises: The six sheaths are associated with cognition.
Some thinkers assign cognitive status to each sheath individually.
Others hold that one sheath functions with the assistance of all the others.
mv-k06-v773.inference: There are divergent views on whether cognition belongs to each sheath separately or to one sheath aided by the rest.

mv-k06-v774.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v774.question: What further opinions exist about how the sheaths operate in cognition?
premises: Thinkers disagree about the cognitive role of the six sheaths.
Some propose occasional or situational operation of particular sheaths.
Others propose operation by pairs or by combinations of triads and pairs.
mv-k06-v774.inference: The sheaths are variously explained as operating situationally, in pairs, or in mixed combinations.

mv-k06-v775.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v775.question: What different views identify the means of valid cognition?
premises: Some hold valid cognition arises from mutual favoring.
Others hold it arises from mutual cognition.
Still others hold primordial nature of balanced qualities alone is valid cognition.
mv-k06-v775.inference: Thinkers disagree about whether valid cognition is mutual, cognitive, or identical with primordial nature.
uncertainties: The exact referents of the mutual favoring and mutual cognition are not specified in this verse alone.

mv-k06-v776.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v776.question: Why do some regard primordial nature as the primary knower?
premises: They cite experiences of sleep, intoxication, and fainting.
In such states the knower appears as if asleep.
Wherever this condition holds, that state is taken as the knower.
mv-k06-v776.inference: The persistence of a dormant subject in altered states is used to identify primordial nature as the primary knower.
uncertainties: The boundary between the knower and primordial nature is implied rather than explicitly defined.

mv-k06-v777.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v777.question: What makes that state count as knowerhood in deep sleep?
premises: In such deep sleep, cognition and object are not apprehended.
The elements involved are taken as mutually unchanging.
Because of this, that alone is identified as the knowerhood of the subject.
mv-k06-v777.inference: Knowerhood is attributed to that underlying state when cognition and object are absent and no change is admitted.
uncertainties: The verse compresses the argument and leaves the identity of the unchanging relata implicit.

mv-k06-v778.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v778.question: What is taken as primary cognition in that account?
premises: Primordial nature alone conceives 'I know'.
In that account, the primary cognition is distinguished from that conceit.
Primary cognition is the seeing that belongs to spirit alone.
mv-k06-v778.inference: The view separates primordial nature's conceit of knowing from the primary cognition proper to spirit.
uncertainties: The verse states the distinction briefly and does not explain how spirit's seeing relates to prakṛti.

mv-k06-v779.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v779.question: How do some thinkers characterize that primary cognition?
premises: That cognition is described as pure and unchanging.
It is described as free from the forms of being and nonbeing.
Some maintain this view by relying on a Sāṃkhya framework.
mv-k06-v779.inference: A Sāṃkhya-influenced position treats primary cognition as pure, immutable, and beyond being and nonbeing.
uncertainties: The phrase 'Sāṃkhya covering' may be descriptive or mildly polemical; the verse does not make the tone explicit.

mv-k06-v780.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v780.question: What do another group identify as the means of cognition?
premises: Another group is described as living on knowledge in the house of the teacher Vayya.
They identify the level of intellect as the means of cognition.
That intellect-level is characterized as colored by seer and seen.
mv-k06-v780.inference: This group locates valid cognition in an intellect that is conditioned by both subject and object.
uncertainties: The historical identity of the teacher Vayya is not recoverable from the verse alone.

mv-k06-v781.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v781.question: Which further candidates are proposed as valid cognition?
premises: Some followers of Paramarshi call the collection of its modifications valid cognition.
Others identify valid cognition with the class of properties counted as eight beginning with merit.
Both views shift valid cognition away from a single simple locus.
mv-k06-v781.inference: Different schools treat either mental modifications or a set of properties as the basis of valid cognition.
uncertainties: The antecedent of 'its modifications' is not explicit in this verse and depends on the preceding discussion.

mv-k06-v782.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v782.question: Which inner faculties are proposed as the locus of cognition?
premises: Some identify cognition with ego-sense alone.
Some identify it with intellect and others with mind.
Some hold that all three operate equally everywhere.
mv-k06-v782.inference: The inner instrument is variously located in ego, intellect, mind, or their combined functioning.

mv-k06-v783.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v783.question: Do the sense organs function singly or together as cognition?
premises: Some accept each one of the ten sense organs as a means of cognition.
Others accept all these sense organs together.
The latter appeal to their unconfused functioning everywhere.
mv-k06-v783.inference: The senses are proposed either as individually sufficient or as collectively operative in cognition.

mv-k06-v784.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v784.question: How can a blind person still be affected by visual information?
premises: Even a blind person has some domain of form.
That domain can produce a change when it reaches the hearing sense.
The other senses may remain in an equal, unaffected condition.
mv-k06-v784.inference: The argument claims that form can still be present and effective even without direct visual functioning.
uncertainties: The mechanism by which form affects hearing is compressed and not fully explained.

mv-k06-v785.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v785.question: What example shows a blind person responding to a visual description?
premises: A blind person hears that dawn has come and the sky is clear of clouds.
On a wintry day this report brings great satisfaction.
The response occurs without direct visual perception.
mv-k06-v785.inference: The example supports the claim that nonvisual cognition can still engage with form-related content.

mv-k06-v786.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v786.question: Does the blind person's satisfaction amount to direct awareness of form?
premises: The blind person may infer comfort arising from the removal of cold.
Even so, his own awareness does not illuminate form.
Inference and direct form-awareness are distinguished.
mv-k06-v786.inference: The example does not establish direct visual cognition in the blind person, only an indirect awareness.

mv-k06-v787.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v787.question: Why do some locate valid cognition in the subtle elements?
premises: Some accept the subtle elements as the locus of valid cognition.
They appeal to rules such as the eye-ray not making contact.
These considerations are used to support cognition at the subtle-element level.
mv-k06-v787.inference: The subtle elements are proposed as the operative basis of cognition because direct sensory contact is questioned.
uncertainties: The referenced rules are only indicated by 'and so on' and not spelled out in this verse.

mv-k06-v788.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v788.question: What follows from the claimed invisibility of the sense organs?
premises: The invisibility of the eye and other senses is said to be explained by that view.
With respect to a yogin, such invisibility is said never to be explained.
The same property is treated differently for ordinary and yogic cases.
mv-k06-v788.inference: The proposed account explains ordinary sensory invisibility but fails when extended to the yogin.
uncertainties: The verse assumes a background theory of yogic perception without stating it explicitly.

mv-k06-v789.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v789.question: Can gross elements or even the object be valid cognition?
premises: Some declare the gross luminous elements to be valid cognition.
Others accept even the object of cognition as valid cognition.
Both views extend validity beyond the inner faculties.
mv-k06-v789.inference: The debate expands to include external elements and even the cognized object as candidates for valid cognition.
uncertainties: The relation between 'gross elements' and 'luminous ones' is compact in the compound and may reflect a specific doctrinal grouping.

mv-k06-v790.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v790.question: Why would objects like a pot count as valid cognition?
premises: The position states that whatever gives rise to knowerhood is valid cognition.
A pot and similar objects give rise to knowerhood.
Therefore those objects are also regarded as valid cognition.
mv-k06-v790.inference: If knowerhood is the criterion, then the objects that occasion it are included as valid cognition.

mv-k06-v791.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v791.question: Does ordinary language settle what counts as valid cognition?
premises: Ordinary usage does not follow the nature of reality.
It is formed largely by mere convention or wish.
Therefore it is mostly figurative.
mv-k06-v791.inference: Ordinary linguistic usage cannot by itself determine the true locus of valid cognition.

mv-k06-v792.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v792.question: How does ordinary speech attribute knowing to an object?
premises: Someone is asked how he knows.
He replies that he knows by this seen pot.
Ordinary speech thus credits the object in the act of knowing.
mv-k06-v792.inference: Common language can make the object appear to be the means of knowing, but this reflects usage rather than strict analysis.

mv-k06-v793.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v793.question: Is assigning cognition to the object a decisive fault?
premises: Even if cognition is attributed to the object, that is not outside ordinary usage.
In a root-level doctrine of non-difference, contradiction is not automatically a fault.
The objection from contradiction is therefore limited.
mv-k06-v793.inference: The attribution of cognition to the object is not conclusively refuted, especially within a non-difference framework.
uncertainties: The verse is compressed and polemical; the exact scope of 'root-level doctrine of non-difference' is not fully specified.

mv-k06-v794.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v794.question: What follows if valid cognition is identified with its total causal complex?
premises: Some identify valid cognition with the totality of its causal factors.
By doing so they clearly accept the cognitive status of the object and other factors.
If that status belongs to the aggregate, it cannot be denied to its members without explanation.
mv-k06-v794.inference: Treating the causal aggregate as valid cognition implicitly grants cognitive status to the object and related factors.

mv-k06-v795.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v795.question: How do some thinkers describe cognition across all distinctions?
premises: Some assign cognitive status to every distinction of every measured thing.
They say this cognition arises in sequence everywhere.
They also allow that in some cases it arises without sequence.
mv-k06-v795.inference: This view treats cognition as operating through all distinctions, sometimes sequentially and sometimes non-sequentially.
uncertainties: The compressed compound in token 3 is doctrinally dense; the gloss follows the most direct reading.

mv-k06-v796.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v796.question: How is that comprehensive view of cognition presented here?
premises: Some hold that in certain cases cognition is full with a complete grasp of both sequence and nonsequence.
The text introduces this as their view.
Here that view is presented only by a brief indication.
mv-k06-v796.inference: The doctrine of cognition encompassing both sequence and nonsequence is acknowledged but only sketched in this passage.

mv-k06-v797.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v797.question: What is the first stage in the process being outlined?
premises: First there is contact with the object.
That contact appears suddenly.
It occurs through an inquiry into the intent concerning another seen thing.
mv-k06-v797.inference: The initial stage of cognition is described as a sudden object-contact shaped by an outwardly directed inquiry.
uncertainties: The long compound in token 5 is syntactically compressed; the reading follows the surface sequence.

mv-k06-v798.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v798.question: What culminates the cognitive process described in this sequence?
premises: Knowerhood is described as the final stage.
There is an unfolding of the eye.
Then there is an inner brightening through the unfolding of mind, ego, and intellect.
mv-k06-v798.inference: The process culminates in knowerhood through successive unfoldings of sense and inner faculties.
uncertainties: The final compound is dense; the gloss preserves the sequence of faculties and unfolding without adding unstated relations.

mv-k06-v799.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v799.question: What arises after the effulgence of purified masculine consciousness?
premises: After that comes the radiance of purified masculine consciousness.
Then arise the limiting nights of time, limitation, attachment, impurity, and ignorance.
These limiting factors appear in sequence.
mv-k06-v799.inference: The emergence of purified masculine consciousness is followed sequentially by the manifestation of the five limiting factors.
uncertainties: The exact nuance of pauṃsna in this context is interpretive.

mv-k06-v800.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v800.question: In what different combinations can these factors arise at the limited level?
premises: The limiting factors may arise otherwise or together.
They may arise in pairs, in threes, or all together.
They may even arise by combinations of four or five at the limited level.
mv-k06-v800.inference: At the limited level, the limiting factors can manifest in multiple possible groupings rather than in only one fixed order.

mv-k06-v801.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v801.question: What kinds of doubts arise in that limited condition?
premises: In that state, doubts arise.
These doubts concern nonbeing, agency, attachment, proof, and reasoning.
They appear variegated according to different sequences.
mv-k06-v801.inference: The limited condition gives rise to multiple forms of doubt whose character varies with the order of manifestation.

mv-k06-v802.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v802.question: What becomes the valid means of knowledge at the culminating stage?
premises: After that stage comes a nonconceptual knowledge.
This knowledge reveals pure sovereignty.
In the final state of cognition, it attains the status of a valid means of knowledge.
mv-k06-v802.inference: At the culminating cognitive stage, nonconceptual knowledge that reveals pure sovereignty functions as valid knowledge.

mv-k06-v803.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v803.question: How does the knower attain fullness in the Sadashiva state?
premises: Then the knower rests on the noble powers of knowledge and will of Sadashiva.
That knower attains fullness.
This fullness is fulfilled in the path that culminates in Shakti.
mv-k06-v803.inference: By resting on Sadashiva's knowledge and will powers, the knower reaches fullness at the culmination of the path in Shakti.

mv-k06-v804.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v804.question: Why does differentiated awareness arise if knowerhood is full?
premises: Full knowerhood shines forth equally.
Differentiated forms of awareness arise from nonseparation from concealment of some part of that fullness.
Thus differentiation does not negate the underlying fullness.
mv-k06-v804.inference: Even when knowerhood is full, differentiated awareness appears because some aspect of that fullness is not separated from concealment.

mv-k06-v805.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v805.question: Why do those who do not know fail to recognize the scriptural state?
premises: The distinctions of clarity and otherness in awareness become countless.
Because of this multiplicity, the underlying state is obscured.
Those who do not know therefore fail to recognize the state taught in the Shiva scriptures.
mv-k06-v805.inference: The countless differentiations of awareness prevent the ignorant from recognizing the state described in the Shiva scriptures.

mv-k06-v806.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v806.question: Why can reasoning and reflection not operate in rapid or subtle states of awareness?
premises: Awareness appears as clear, unclear, remembered, forgotten, and in states like deep sleep.
These states can occur with great rapidity.
In such rapidity, reasoning and reflective discernment are not possible.
mv-k06-v806.inference: Because these states of awareness can arise too quickly or subtly, reasoning and reflection cannot function there.

mv-k06-v807.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v807.question: Do explanatory constructs like attention and impressions truly explain this state?
premises: Mental attention, mental impressions, and unseen merit are proposed as explanations.
These are clearly just words in this context.
Here they do not establish a real explanatory meaning.
mv-k06-v807.inference: Appeals to attention, impressions, or unseen factors fail to provide a genuine explanation of the state in question.
uncertainties: The token '...' marks a textual gap and the exact missing content is uncertain.
The form 'tatri' is unusual and may reflect the transmitted text.

mv-k06-v808.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v808.question: What happens to lower principles when higher principles function as the measure?
premises: Higher and higher principles can function as the measure.
When that status is determined, lower principles are viewed in relation to them.
The lower and lower principles then take on the status of objects.
mv-k06-v808.inference: When higher principles serve as the measuring subject, the lower principles become the measured objects.

mv-k06-v809.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v809.question: Is there any sequence in the direct apprehension of that awareness?
premises: No sequence exists here because interruption would be possible only if there were mediation.
Neither knowledge nor the intellectual faculty perceives that awareness as an external object.
Direct awareness is not apprehended through a mediated sequence.
mv-k06-v809.inference: There is no temporal or mediated sequence in the apprehension of that awareness because it is not grasped by knowledge or intellect as an object.

mv-k06-v810.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v810.question: How are discriminative knowledge and the external sense faculty characterized?
premises: Knowledge is declared to be discriminating.
That discriminating knowledge rests upon the intellect.
The external sense faculty has the nature of light and consists in perception.
mv-k06-v810.inference: Discriminative knowledge operates through the intellect, while the external sense faculty functions as perceptual illumination.

mv-k06-v811.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v811.question: What functions are assigned to mind, ego, intellect, and knowledge?
premises: Mind is declared to function for conception.
Ego-making is appropriating, and intellect is determining.
Knowledge there is also discriminating.
mv-k06-v811.inference: The inner faculties are distinguished by their functions: conception, appropriation, determination, and discrimination.

mv-k06-v812.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v812.question: How are attachment, limitation, time, and restriction characterized in that system?
premises: Attachment is described as coloring.
Limitation shows capacity, and time delimits the agent.
Restriction is described as regulating.
mv-k06-v812.inference: The limiting principles function by coloring, enabling limited capacity, delimiting agency, and regulating experience.
uncertainties: The form 'vyavacchit' is terse and may be elliptical in the transmitted text.

mv-k06-v813.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v813.question: How does maya function in relation to knowers and objects?
premises: Maya is reflective in nature.
It manifests commonness with other knowers.
It reflects the sphere of objects and their various graspers.
mv-k06-v813.inference: Maya produces differentiated cognition by presenting shared objectivity and multiple knowers and objects.

mv-k06-v814.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v814.question: How are maya and pure knowledge contrasted in their effects?
premises: Maya causes agitation and a fall from the enjoyment of fullness.
Pure knowledge gives rest in fullness.
Pure knowledge has the nature of auspicious Shiva.
mv-k06-v814.inference: Maya disturbs the experience of fullness, whereas pure knowledge restores repose in fullness as Shiva-nature.

mv-k06-v815.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v815.question: What is the role of the power of will in this account?
premises: The power of will reflects a nature filled with the aspect of knowledge.
It manifests the full being of the knower aspect.
Thus it participates in the fullness of subjectivity.
mv-k06-v815.inference: The power of will discloses the knower's fullness by reflecting a nature saturated with knowledge.

mv-k06-v816.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v816.question: How does the full state of the knower unfold through cognitive stages?
premises: Relying on the relevant powers, the state of the knower becomes completely full.
This full knower-state unfolds in stages.
First come illumination and perception, then conception and intention.
mv-k06-v816.inference: The full knower-state manifests through an ordered unfolding of cognitive functions beginning with illumination and perception.
uncertainties: The token 'ṝü' appears to be a textual marker rather than a lexical word.

mv-k06-v817.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v817.question: What further stages follow in the unfolding of the knower-state?
premises: After the earlier stages come determination and subsequent seeing.
Then appear discrimination and nonattachment as a pair.
This is followed by delimitation of agency and manifestation of commonness.
mv-k06-v817.inference: The knower-state continues to unfold through determination, discrimination, delimited agency, and shared manifestation.

mv-k06-v818.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v818.question: What is the culminating recognition in this unfolding of awareness?
premises: There is presentation of the full object stirred by various reflections.
There is awareness of full knowerhood.
This awareness is indeed the Bhairava state.
mv-k06-v818.inference: The culmination of the unfolding is the recognition that full knowerhood, even amid varied reflection, is the Bhairava state.

mv-k06-v819.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v819.question: How is the moon of consciousness described in its sixteenfold manifestation?
premises: The object-domain is manifested in sixteen ways.
As long as this sixteenfold manifestation occurs, the moon of consciousness is present.
That moon of consciousness is declared to abide in sixteen phases.
mv-k06-v819.inference: The moon of consciousness is characterized by a sixteenfold mode of manifestation corresponding to the object-domain.

mv-k06-v820.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v820.question: What sixfold sequence is established at the beginning of this process?
premises: The unsurpassed state comes first.
It is followed by bliss, will, and lordship.
Then come arising, inclination, and immersion, forming a group of six.
mv-k06-v820.inference: The process begins with a sixfold sequence starting from the unsurpassed state and moving through bliss, will, lordship, arising, inclination, and immersion.

mv-k06-v821.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v821.question: How does will relate to knowledge and action in this sequence?
premises: The sequence runs from the unsurpassed to the power of knowledge.
Will itself is established in that process.
Will, together with lordship, is established in relation to the power of action.
mv-k06-v821.inference: Within the sequence from the unsurpassed to knowledge, will becomes established as the link to action through lordship.

mv-k06-v822.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v822.question: Why does the sequence beginning with will attain a sixfold state?
premises: A subtle portion of light and stability is taken up.
By taking that up, the process attains a sixfold state.
The series beginning with will is connected with the prior unsurpassed and bliss.
mv-k06-v822.inference: The will-series becomes sixfold because it takes up a subtle aspect of light and stability while remaining connected to the unsurpassed and bliss.
uncertainties: The token 'ṝü' appears to be a textual marker rather than a lexical word.

mv-k06-v823.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v823.question: How do the juncture syllables and the bindu state arise in this sequence?
premises: Connection with that and related elements produces a group of four juncture syllables.
From that arises attainment of awareness of one's own nature.
From that attainment arises a state beginning with bindu.
mv-k06-v823.inference: The sequence moves from juncture syllables to self-awareness and then to the bindu-level state.
uncertainties: The exact referent of tadādi is not explicit in this verse alone.

mv-k06-v824.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v824.question: What is the śākta visarga that arises at this stage?
premises: After the previous stage, a form filled with the whole sequence appears.
In that state arises the śākta visarga.
This visarga is remembered as projection.
mv-k06-v824.inference: The śākta visarga is identified with the power of projection.

mv-k06-v825.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v825.question: How is the separation of visarga counted among the kalās?
premises: The separation of visarga itself is called the seventeenth kalā.
In some cases that same phase is counted as the eighteenth.
The shift to eighteenth is due to connection with agitation.
mv-k06-v825.inference: The same visarga-separation phase can be counted as seventeenth or eighteenth depending on agitation.

mv-k06-v826.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v826.question: What is the supreme kaula power of the supreme akula?
premises: The supreme akula is identified with the supreme letter a in the form of supreme Bhairava.
That akula has a supreme kaula power.
This power is described as the highest.
mv-k06-v826.inference: The highest kaula power belongs to the supreme akula, the letter a as supreme Bhairava.

mv-k06-v827.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v827.question: How does visarga give rise to the world and its agitation?
premises: That very power is identified as visarga.
From that visarga this world is born.
Its capacity for agitation is the arising of the stir of agitation.
mv-k06-v827.inference: Visarga is the source of the world and of the agitation that unfolds within it.

mv-k06-v828.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v828.question: What arises when agitation is not yet fully unfolded?
premises: Agitation may lack fullness.
From that lack there is a bending into the sequence of that akula.
This movement arises from the swaying reflection of the sixfold nature.
mv-k06-v828.inference: Incomplete agitation turns the process back toward akula through the reflective oscillation of the sixfold.
uncertainties: The exact technical sense of ṣaṭka in this verse is not specified.

mv-k06-v829.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v829.question: Whose unfolding is this process, and what is its inner nature?
premises: Because it is of supreme nature, the unfolding belongs to the first alone.
That same one is the Lord.
The Lord is inwardly always of a flashing-forth nature.
mv-k06-v829.inference: The entire unfolding is the inner, ever-flashing manifestation of the supreme Lord.

mv-k06-v830.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v830.question: How is the Lord described in his inner fullness and outward beauty?
premises: The Lord possesses the middle power filled with all inner beings.
From the nature of his own willed agitation arises the bliss of the world.
That arising bliss makes him beautiful.
mv-k06-v830.inference: The Lord's inner fullness and self-willed agitation manifest as the blissful beauty of the world.

mv-k06-v831.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v831.question: What is the union of Śiva and Śakti called in this state?
premises: The Lord always flashes forth, beautiful with the rasa of full emission.
There is a union of Śiva and Śakti.
That union is called love.
mv-k06-v831.inference: The ever-flashing fullness of emission is expressed as the loving union of Śiva and Śakti.

mv-k06-v832.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v832.question: How do practitioners seek entry into the state of full emission?
premises: The state of full emission is a locus of entry.
Practitioners seek to attain entry there.
They do so through the tradition of licking, churning, and related practices.
mv-k06-v832.inference: Entry into full emission is pursued through specific transmitted practices.
uncertainties: The technical ritual meanings of lehana and manthana are not explained in this verse.

mv-k06-v833.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v833.question: How does supreme radiance move through the body in this process?
premises: The middle channel is established as the locus.
Supreme radiance vitalizes the whole body.
This occurs from the midst of agitated nectar.
mv-k06-v833.inference: Supreme radiance, arising from agitated nectar, vitalizes the whole body through the middle channel.

mv-k06-v834.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v834.question: What distinguishes incomplete emission from full emission?
premises: The process moves toward the state of emission and reaches the wonder of bliss.
When merely incomplete, it remains limited.
When full, it is wholly of the Lord.
mv-k06-v834.inference: Full emission culminates not just in bliss but in a state wholly pervaded by the Lord.

mv-k06-v835.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v835.question: Why does the single power of emission unfold as agitation?
premises: The power of emission is one.
That same power unfolds.
Its unfolding as agitation occurs because effort is doubled.
mv-k06-v835.inference: Agitated emission is not a second power but the one emissive power intensified by doubled effort.
uncertainties: The precise technical meaning of prayatna-dviguṇatva is not fully specified.

mv-k06-v836.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v836.question: What role does the letter ha play in the generation of consonants?
premises: The letter ha is the producer of all consonants.
That same ha, by connection with bindu, returns to its own level.
Its generative role is linked to this return.
mv-k06-v836.inference: Ha generates the consonants and, joined with bindu, reverts to its own foundational level.

mv-k06-v837.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v837.question: What supreme state does ha reach, and what consonants arise there?
premises: Ha resorts to the supreme level.
That supreme level is accepted here as the I-sense.
From that locus arise ka born of a and another born of i.
mv-k06-v837.inference: The return of ha to the supreme I-sense grounds the emergence of ka and the i-born consonant.
uncertainties: The identity of the i-born consonant is implied but not named in this verse.

mv-k06-v838.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v838.question: How do the ṭa and ta classes arise from earlier phonetic conditions?
premises: From the limiting condition of the shadow of the repha part, linked to ṛ, arises the ṭa class.
From that same source, through dha, another sequence proceeds.
The progression follows the order of limiting shadow conditions.
mv-k06-v838.inference: The ṭa and subsequent ta classes emerge through successive phonetic shadow conditions rooted in earlier sounds.
uncertainties: The exact phonetic derivation of dharāc in this chain is compressed and partly implicit.

mv-k06-v839.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v839.question: In what order do the ta class and semivowels arise?
premises: After the previous stage comes the ta class.
Then arise ya, ra, la beginning with u, and va.
These arise in order from the i-class and from u.
mv-k06-v839.inference: The ta class and the semivowels emerge in a fixed phonetic sequence grounded in i and u.

mv-k06-v840.speaker: Abhinavagupta (teacher voice)
mv-k06-v840.question: How do the semivowels and sibilants arise from the letter i?
premises: The semivowels are reached in this sequence.
From the letter i, in two divisions, arise śa, ṣa, and sa.
Their arising is joined with phases of pure limiting conditions.
mv-k06-v840.inference: The letter i serves as a source for both the semivowels and the twofold emergence of the sibilants.
